title: Micro-Goals Get Projects and People Back on Track
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses stalled or slow-moving team members by proposing a fix rooted in scale: breaking a distant, intimidating objective into a single small, achievable next step rather than a full roadmap. It explains the psychological mechanism, arguing micro-goals bypass perfectionism, procrastination, and anxiety by lowering the size of the next required action, and that small wins build momentum that struggling team members otherwise lack. Leaders are advised to resist offering more than one micro-goal at a time when someone is genuinely stuck, waiting for each success before assigning the next step. The piece closes with the memorable claim that the smallest goal can produce the largest motivation.
points: Micro-goals work by lowering the size of the immediate task, which bypasses the perfectionism, procrastination, and anxiety that stall struggling team members.
Leaders should offer only one micro-goal at a time to someone who is genuinely stuck, rather than a full multi-step plan.
Small, sequential wins are argued to build the momentum less effective team members need to eventually identify their own next steps.
The core claim is counterintuitive: the smallest possible goal can produce the largest motivational effect.
quotes: Team members who are stalled, delayed, or slow typically have lost sight of these steps or have failed to focus on the micro-steps or goals that make them up.
Instead of focusing on a distant and somewhat intimidating objective, micro-goals break that objective down into tiny, actionable tasks that can be completed more easily and quickly.
Studies show that micro-goals bypass the psychological barriers some team members experience when approaching a larger task.
When team members are really lost or stuck, good leaders avoid the temptation to point to more than one micro-goal at a time.
The best leaders know that the smallest goal can sometimes be the largest motivation.
